newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN envoy on missing in former Yugoslavia resigns.
newsitem.headline: UN envoy on missing in former Yugoslavia resigns.

text.p: The U.N. expert who led attempts to determine the fate of tens of thousands of people missing in war-torn former Yugoslavia resigned in frustration on Wednesday, complaining that he had never received the necessary political and financial support.

Manfred Nowak, Austrian chairman of the U.N. working group on enforced disappearances, said the "non-cooperative attitude of Belgrade" remained a major reason for the lack of progress in clarifying the fate of some 25,000 missing in the region.

Most of the 20,000 persons missing in Bosnia and 5,000 missing in Croatia "most probably" had been killed, Nowak said in a speech to the U.N. Human Rights Commission holding its annual six-week meeting in Geneva.

But families deserved to know the fate of their loved ones, the great majority of whom were Bosnian Moslem victims of "ethnic cleansing" by the Yugoslav National Army (JNA), Serb paramilitary groups and Bosnian Serb forces, he said.

"If we wish to tell the women of Srebrenica or other families of missing persons the truth and facilitate a decent burial of their loved ones, then the international community should take the lead by organising such exhumations with the assistance of Bosnian and international teams of forensic experts," he said.

Nowak was referring to the Moslem enclave of Srebrenica in eastern Bosnia which, despite being a U.N.-proclaimed safe haven, was overrun in July 1995 by Bosnian Serbs, who expelled some 40,000 people. Almost 8,000 men remain unaccounted for nearly two years later.

In Croatia, where 5,000 are still missing, the figure includes more than 2,500 Croatian civilians and combatants who suffered "ethnic cleansing" by the JNA and Serb paramilitary groups, 1,000 JNA soldiers and up to 2,000 Croatian Serb civilians who allegedly disappeared as a result of Croatian army operations.

Nowak said that, since his appeal last year to donor countries for $6 million to excavate mass graves, mostly in the territory of the Bosnian Serb entity, Republika Srpska, and to exhume and identify human remains, he had received only $300,000.
"My resignation is, unfortunately, not due to the fact that the fate and whereabouts of many thousands of missing persons in the region were clarified," Nowak said.

"On the contrary, the number of missing persons has significantly increased during these three years, and the families are still waiting in vain for an answer from the authorities concerned and the international community on the fate of their loved ones," he added.

Nowak complained of insufficient political will to establish the fate of the missing, but suggested that a so-called "Blue Ribbon Commission", set up at the initiative of the United States, seemed to have better support and might be more successful.

"Most suspected mass graves are located in the territory of the Republika Srpska, and the Bosnian Serb authorities are not willing to open them unless there is a specific interest of reciprocity vis-a-vis the (Bosnian-Croat) Federation authorities," he added.
